content.overview: Where a company has given a preference to a creditor, surety or guarantor by doing or suffering anything that puts that person in a better position in the event of liquidation than if the act had not been done, and the preference occurred within six months before the winding-up application, the Tribunal may order restoration of the prior position if it is satisfied the transaction is a fraudulent preference.
content.glance: Tribunal may set aside fraudulent preferences given within six months before the winding-up application and restore the status quo.
content.study: Section 328 targets preferences that improve a creditor’s (or surety/guarantor’s) position in a prospective liquidation. The preference must have occurred prior to six months of making the winding-up application. If the Tribunal is satisfied the transaction is a fraudulent preference, it may make such order as it thinks fit to restore the position to what it would have been if the preference had not been given. Sub-section (2) separately empowers the Tribunal, where there is a preference transfer of property, delivery of goods, payment or execution within six months before the winding-up application, to declare the transaction invalid and restore the position. The provision is part of the avoidance regime in Chapter XX and must be read with the IBC avoidance provisions where the process is under the Code.

sections.heading: Fraudulent preference
sections.body: Preference to a creditor, surety or guarantor that improves that person’s position in liquidation, effected within six months before the winding-up application; Tribunal may order restoration.

sections.heading: Related transfers within six months
sections.body: Preference transfer of property, delivery of goods, payment or execution within six months before the application may be declared invalid and the position restored.

examples.title: Preferential repayment
examples.body: Three months before a winding-up petition is filed, the company repays in full an unsecured debt to a favoured creditor while other unsecured creditors remain unpaid. If the Tribunal finds the repayment put that creditor in a better position than he would otherwise have occupied in liquidation, it may order restoration under s. 328.

hypotheticals.question: Can a repayment made five months before the winding-up application be set aside?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes, if it constitutes a preference to a creditor (or surety/guarantor) that improves that person’s position in liquidation and the Tribunal is satisfied it is a fraudulent preference; the six-month window is satisfied.

misconceptions.trap: Any payment to a creditor within six months is automatically void.
misconceptions.correction: The Tribunal must be satisfied that the transaction is a fraudulent preference that improves the recipient’s position in liquidation; the order is discretionary restoration.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 328 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the act alleged to be a preference and the six-month window. II. Assess improvement of position in liquidation. III. Consider Tribunal’s restoration power.
